name: Sarrus linkage
summary: Two hinged limbs set at right angles join a base and a top plate, so the top plate can only move straight up and down with no slide.

ratio.typical: plate height h = 2L cos(theta), up to 2L

topology.notes: base, top plate and two limbs of two links each; overconstrained, the Grubler count gives 0 but the two limbs share the one vertical freedom

explain.motion: Each limb is two equal links hinged to the base, to each other at a knee, and to the top plate, with all three hinge axes of a limb parallel. One limb alone lets the top plate move in one vertical plane; the second limb, turned 90 degrees, only allows motion in a plane at right angles. The only motion both allow is straight up and down, so the top plate rises along an exact line as the knees fold.
explain.forces: A vertical load on the plate becomes compression or tension in the limb links and a bending moment at the knees; near full extension the links are almost straight and carry large loads with little torque. Side loads and twisting are resisted by the hinges of the crossed limb, so hinge play shows up as wobble.
explain.benefits: An exact straight line with only revolute hinges, no guide rails, and the plates stay parallel with no rotation.
explain.limits: Travel is limited to less than twice the link length and the hinges must be stiff and accurate because the linkage is overconstrained. At full extension the knees reach a singular, straight position from which it cannot be driven back by a vertical push alone.

build.input: lower link of limb 1, rocking about its base hinge (theta from vertical 10° to 80°)
build.output: top plate height h above the base, and its straight-line path

members.def: square plate 80 x 80, hinge lines on two adjacent edges
limb 1 lower link, base hinge to knee K1, length L
limb 1 upper link, knee K1 to top plate, length L
limb 2 lower link, base hinge to knee K2, length L, hinge axes at 90° to limb 1
limb 2 upper link, knee K2 to top plate, length L
top plate 80 x 80, parallel to base

params.name: theta
params.note: lower link angle from vertical, default pose

params.name: limb_angle
params.note: angle between the two limb hinge planes

build.defining_relations: Within each limb all three hinge axes are parallel; the two limbs' axes are not parallel (90° here). With equal links the knee lies at horizontal offset L sin(theta) and the plate height is h = 2L cos(theta); the plate translates with zero rotation and zero sideways motion.
build.range: theta 10° to 80°; plate height 118.2 mm down to 20.8 mm, stroke about 97 mm along a straight vertical line
build.plot: top plate height h vs input link angle theta
build.notes: Draw in pseudo-3D: the two limbs sit on adjacent faces of the plates. Both knees fold outward by the same angle theta. Avoid theta = 0 (straight limbs, singular) and theta = 90° (plates collide).

examples.detail: Compact lifting stages and vertical guides where a slide would bind or need lubrication.
Built as a folded flexure linkage for small exact vertical motions in robotics and prototyping.
Used as the folding wall unit of deployable boxes and lift platforms.

references.title: Construction of Some Useful Linkages (UC Berkeley, R. Fearing)

name: Tusi couple
summary: A gear rolling inside a ring twice its size: every point on its pitch circle moves in a perfectly straight line.

ratio.typical: stroke = ring pitch diameter = 4 x planet pitch radius (128 mm here)

topology.notes: ground with fixed 32T ring, carrier arm, 16T planet; one internal gear mesh

explain.motion: The arm carries the small gear around inside the fixed ring. Because the ring has exactly twice as many teeth, the small gear spins backwards once for each orbit, and any point on its pitch circle slides back and forth along a diameter of the ring. The two tracers here move on two straight lines at right angles.
explain.forces: Driving torque on the arm becomes a tangential tooth force against the ring, which turns the small gear. A load on the traced point acts through the gear's own pin and teeth, so there is no sliding guide at all, only rolling contact. Near the ends of the stroke the arm has little leverage on the tracer, so it cannot be driven from the tracer there.
explain.benefits: An exact straight line, and exact simple harmonic motion along it, from purely rotating parts.
explain.limits: Needs an accurate internal gear pair with exactly 2:1 teeth, and backlash shows up directly as error in the line. Points inside the pitch circle trace ellipses, not lines, so the tracer must sit exactly on the pitch circle.

build.ground: ring gear, 32T module 4 (pitch radius 64 mm), centre O
build.output: tracers X and Y on the planet pitch circle, positions along the x and y diameters

members.def: internal gear 32T m4, pitch radius R = 64
carrier O→C, length R - r = 32
spur gear 16T m4, pitch radius r = 32, pinned at C
tracer X on the planet pitch circle, moves along the x axis
tracer Y on the planet pitch circle, 90° round from X, moves along the y axis

build.defining_relations: R = 2r (zr = 2 zp). Planet absolute rotation = -(zr/zp - 1) x arm angle = -u. A point on the planet pitch circle that starts at (R, 0) is at x = R cos(u), y = 0, so it moves on a straight diameter with simple harmonic motion; a point 90° round moves on y = R sin(u). Points at radius rho < r trace ellipses with semi-axes r + rho and r - rho.
build.range: arm 360° continuous; each tracer reciprocates 128 mm (from -64 to +64) per arm turn
build.plot: tracer X position vs arm angle (a pure cosine)
build.notes: Phase the planet so a tooth meshes at u = 0 (the site uses meshIn with tooth phase). Planet spins backwards relative to ground at the same rate as the arm turns forwards.

examples.detail: Matthew Murray used the couple in place of a crosshead guide to turn piston motion into rotation, around 1802.
Al-Tusi used it in 1247 to produce straight-line oscillation from circular motions in astronomy.
Gear-driven Tusi couples make rows of dots slide on lines while appearing to rotate as a circle.

name: Crank and slotted lever quick-return
summary: A crank pin slides in a slotted lever that rocks about a pivot below, pushing a ram slowly forward to cut and pulling it back fast.

ratio.typical: cut:return = (180° + 2 asin(r/d)) : (180° - 2 asin(r/d)), 1.71:1 here; stroke 128 mm

topology.notes: ground, crank, slide block, slotted lever, link, ram; block slides in the lever slot (prismatic), ram on rails (prismatic)

explain.motion: The crank turns at constant speed and its pin, in a sliding block, drives a slotted lever that rocks about a pivot below the crank. The lever swings through the same angle either way, but the crank takes the long way round the circle for the cutting stroke and the short way for the return. A short link at the top of the lever pushes the ram along its rails.
explain.forces: The crank pin pushes the block at right angles to the slot, so the lever sees a torque that is largest when the pin is farthest from the lever pivot, which is during the cut. The cutting load on the ram returns through the link, lever pivot and block; side thrust on the ram goes into the rails.
explain.benefits: Simple, robust and gives a slow, nearly uniform cutting stroke with a quick idle return, saving cycle time.
explain.limits: Ram speed is not constant during the cut, and the block and slot wear and need lubrication. The time ratio is fixed by r/d; changing stroke by changing r also changes the ratio.

build.ground: frame with crank bearing O2 at (0, 0), lever pivot O3 at (0, -100), ram rails on y = 64
build.output: ram position x along the rails

members.def: slide block on crank pin A, sliding in the lever slot
slotted lever pivoted at O3, length Ll = 160 to pin B
slider on line y = 64, pinned to link at C
O2, O3, rails

build.defining_relations: Lever angle phi = atan2 of A from O3. Extreme lever positions occur when the slot is tangent to the crank circle: beta = asin(r/d) = 23.58°. Cut angle = 180° + 2 beta = 227.2°, return = 180° - 2 beta = 132.8°, time ratio 1.71:1. Lever swing ±beta; B = O3 + Ll(sin, cos); ram C = (Bx + sqrt(l^2 - (yR - By)^2), yR); stroke = 2 Ll sin(beta) = 128 mm.
build.range: crank 360° continuous; lever rocks ±23.6°; ram stroke 128 mm
build.plot: ram position vs crank angle (slow cut, fast return)
build.notes: Cutting phase is when ((u + beta) mod 360°) < 227.2°. Block rotates with the lever. Keep link short so its angularity barely affects the stroke (By is the same at both extremes, so stroke stays exact).

examples.detail: The bull gear crank pin drives the rocker arm and ram of a column shaper for planing flat and keyway surfaces.
Vertical-ram slotters use the same slotted lever drive for internal keyways.
Some power hacksaws use a quick-return crank so the blade cuts slowly and returns fast.

name: Whitworth quick-return
summary: A crank pin drives a slotted lever that turns fully round an offset pivot, so a rod-driven ram cuts slowly and returns quickly.

ratio.typical: cut:return = (180° + 2 asin(e/r)) : (180° - 2 asin(e/r)), 1.59:1 here; stroke = 2R = 64 mm

topology.notes: ground, 16T pinion, 50T bull gear (crank), slide block, slotted lever, rod, ram; one gear mesh

explain.motion: A pinion drives the bull gear, whose crank pin carries a block sliding in a slotted lever. The lever pivot sits inside the crank circle, offset by e, so the lever turns a full revolution but at varying speed. A short arm on the far side of the lever drives a connecting rod and ram, which moves slowly while the lever turns the long way and quickly on the short way.
explain.forces: Torque flows from pinion to bull gear, then as a normal force from the pin block onto the slot walls, then through the lever arm R and rod into the ram. The lever torque from the cutting load is largest when the slot is most tilted, loading the block and offset pivot.
explain.benefits: Smoother lever motion than the oscillating slotted lever, a compact layout with a short lever, and a fixed, reliable time ratio.
explain.limits: The ram speed varies through the stroke, and the time ratio depends only on e/r so it cannot be adjusted on the fly. Slot and block wear add backlash at stroke reversals.

build.ground: frame with bull gear axis O2 at (0, 0), lever pivot O3 at (0, -14), pinion axis at 66 mm from O2, ram line y = -14
build.input: pinion 16T, continuous rotation (bull gear turns 16/50 as fast, opposite way)
build.output: ram position x along the line through O3

members.def: spur gear 16T m2, axis at distance 66 from O2 at 200°
spur gear 50T m2, crank pin A at r = 40 from O2
slide block on pin A, sliding in the lever slot
slotted lever pivoted at O3, slot side through A, arm R = 32 on the opposite side to pin B
B→C, Lr = 100
slider on y = -14 (line through O3)
O2, O3, pinion bearing, rails

params.name: R
params.note: lever arm to rod pin B

build.defining_relations: phi = angle of A seen from O3; B = O3 - R(cos phi, sin phi); C = (Bx + sqrt(Lr^2 - (By + e)^2), -e). Ram extremes when the lever is parallel to the ram line, at crank angles where sin = -e/r: beta = asin(e/r) = 20.49°, cut 180° + 2 beta = 221.0°, return 139.0°, ratio 1.59:1. Stroke = 2R = 64 mm. Gear ratio 50/16 = 3.125:1, pinion angle = -(z1/z2) x bull angle + phase.

name: Drag-link quick-return
summary: A double-crank four-bar turns uniform input into uneven output rotation, which drives a ram slowly one way and fast back.

ratio.typical: time ratio about 1.5:1 here (216.5° : 143.5°); stroke about 2 x ram crank radius

topology.notes: ground, input crank, coupler, output crank (with ram arm), connecting rod, ram

explain.motion: The fixed link is the shortest of a Grashof four-bar, so both cranks turn fully round. When the input turns at constant speed, the output crank speeds up over one half turn and slows down over the other. An arm fixed to the output crank drives a connecting rod and ram, and the ram's slow stroke is placed where the output crank is slow.
explain.forces: Torque passes from the input crank through the coupler to the output crank; the transmission angle swings widely, so force transfer is weakest when the coupler and output crank are nearly in line. The ram load comes back through the rod onto the output crank pivot.
explain.benefits: Only pin joints, no slots or sliding blocks except the ram, so it runs quietly and wears little.
explain.limits: The fixed link is short so the pivots crowd together, and the time ratio is modest unless transmission angles become poor (minimum about 30° here).

build.ground: frame with input pivot O2 at (0, 0), output pivot O4 at (25, 0), ram rails on y = 0
build.input: input crank, continuous rotation about O2
build.output: ram position x on the line through O2 and O4

members.def: O4→B, c = 60, carries ram arm O4→D of r = 50 in line with O4→B
slider on y = 0, pinned at E

build.defining_relations: Grashof with the ground shortest: s + l <= p + q (25 + 70 <= 60 + 60) gives a double crank. Output angle from the four-bar loop (open branch). Ram x = r cos(phi4) + sqrt(L^2 - (r sin phi4)^2) measured from O4. Ram extremes at phi4 = 0° and 180°; with these dimensions they occur at input angles about 305.5° and 89.0°, so the slow stroke takes 216.5° of input and the fast stroke 143.5°, ratio 1.51:1. Transmission angle ranges about 30° to 81°.
build.range: input 360° continuous; output crank 360° non-uniform; ram stroke 100 mm
build.plot: ram position vs input crank angle, plus output crank angle vs input angle
build.notes: Keep the same assembly branch throughout (open configuration). Rotating the ram arm relative to O4→B shifts where the slow stroke falls. A ratio near 1.8:1 is possible with d = 30, b = 80, c = 70 but the minimum transmission angle falls to about 22°.

examples.detail: Used as an alternative to the slotted lever to drive a ram with a slow cut and fast return.
Gives a slow, controlled push followed by a fast return on cartoners and feeders.
Provides uneven rotation to time knife or platen motions.

references.title: Kinematics of Machinery question bank and notes (SRM Valliammai)
Drag link quick return, FIRGELLI mechanisms library

name: Offset slider-crank
summary: A slider-crank whose slide line misses the crank centre, so the forward and return strokes take different crank angles.

ratio.typical: stroke slightly over 2r (61.4 mm for r = 30); time ratio 1.09:1 for e = 20

explain.motion: The crank turns at constant speed and the rod pushes a slider along a line that is offset from the crank centre by e. The slider's two dead centres occur where crank and rod are in line, and because of the offset these two crank positions are not 180° apart. One stroke therefore takes slightly more crank angle than the other.
explain.forces: The rod force splits into a useful push along the slide and a side thrust on the guide; offsetting the crank reduces rod angularity during the working stroke, which lowers side thrust and friction there. Near the dead centres the crank has no leverage on the slider.
explain.benefits: The simplest quick-return, with only one more parameter than an ordinary slider-crank, and offset engines (desaxe) gain lower piston side load.
explain.limits: Only small time ratios are practical, as large offsets give poor transmission angles and high side thrust on the return stroke.

build.ground: frame with crank bearing O at (0, 0), slide line y = e
build.output: slider position x along y = e

members.def: crank bearing O and slide guide on y = e
block at B on y = e

params.name: e
params.note: offset of slide line from crank centre

build.defining_relations: x = r cos(theta) + sqrt(l^2 - (e - r sin(theta))^2). Outer dead centre x1 = sqrt((l + r)^2 - e^2) = 128.5; inner x2 = sqrt((l - r)^2 - e^2) = 67.1; stroke = 61.4 mm. Dead-centre crank angles: asin(e/(l + r)) = 8.85° and 180° + asin(e/(l - r)) = 196.6°. alpha = asin(e/(l - r)) - asin(e/(l + r)) = 7.75°; time ratio (180° + alpha)/(180° - alpha) = 1.09:1. Needs r + e < l for full rotation.
build.range: crank 360° continuous; slider stroke 61.4 mm; return stroke takes 172.2° and forward 187.8° of crank angle
build.plot: slider position vs crank angle, with the two dead-centre angles marked
build.notes: Choose the rotation direction so the slower stroke is the working one. Dead centres are singular for driving from the slider.

examples.detail: Some engines and compressors offset the cylinder from the crank to cut piston side thrust on the power stroke.
Small offsets give a slightly slower forward push in packaging pushers.
A standard problem for designing a crank slider to a given time ratio and stroke.

references.title: The Offset Slider Crank: Kinematic Pseudographic Analysis (Int. J. Engng Ed. 1997)

name: Walschaerts valve gear
summary: A steam locomotive linkage that mixes motion from a return crank and the crosshead to time the valve, with reversing and cutoff control.

ratio.typical: valve travel set by die position, about 2 x lap + lead in mid gear up to full travel at full gear

topology.notes: frame, wheel with crank and return crank, main rod, crosshead, eccentric rod, expansion link, radius rod, combination lever, union link, valve spindle, lifting link; die block in curved link slot counted as one higher pair; reverser setting held fixed

explain.motion: A return crank on the driving wheel, set about 90° from the main crank, drives an eccentric rod that rocks the curved expansion link about its trunnion. A die block in the link moves the radius rod, whose end drives the top of the combination lever; the bottom of that lever is driven from the crosshead through the union link. The valve spindle, pinned between them, gets the sum: a lap and lead motion from the crosshead and a variable motion from the link.
explain.forces: Valve friction and steam pressure on the valve flow back through the combination lever into the crosshead and return crank, loads that are small compared with the piston loads. The die block and link slot carry the reversing load and wear most.
explain.benefits: Mounted outside the frames for easy inspection, light, and gives constant lead at all cutoffs, with reversing and cutoff from a single reverser.
explain.limits: Geometry is approximate, so valve events are unequal front and back unless carefully proportioned. Many pins wear and add lost motion.

build.ground: locomotive frame carrying the cylinder, crosshead guides, valve chest guide, expansion link trunnion and reverser
build.input: driving wheel with main crank, continuous rotation
build.output: valve spindle position (valve travel) along the valve chest axis

params.note: expansion link slot radius = radius rod length

params.note: die position in slot, -1 full reverse to +1 full forward, 0 mid gear

build.defining_relations: Valve displacement is approximately x_v = (lap + lead) x crosshead term + k x die x link term: the combination lever gives a component in phase with the piston of size (lap + lead) at the dead centres, and the link adds a component 90° ahead whose size and sign follow the die position. Link slot radius equals radius rod length so moving the die does not move the valve at mid stroke (constant lead). Cutoff shortens as the die approaches the trunnion.

Keep the die block in the slot range. Draw the expansion link arc centred on the radius rod end at mid stroke.

name: Bennett linkage
summary: A four-bar loop with skew hinge axes that still moves with one degree of freedom, thanks to a special balance of lengths and twists.

ratio.typical: tan(th1/2) tan(th2/2) = sin((b + a)/2) / sin((b - a)/2) for twists a, b

topology.notes: spatial 4R, overconstrained: Kutzbach gives -2 but the special geometry gives 1

explain.motion: Four links are joined in a loop by four hinges whose axes are skew, not parallel. Opposite links are equal in length and twist, and the lengths and twists obey a/sin(alpha) = b/sin(beta). With that balance the loop closes in a continuous family of positions, so turning one hinge drives the others, and the whole loop folds and unfolds in space.
explain.forces: Because the mobility depends on exact geometry, loads are shared redundantly across the joints and small errors in length or twist cause binding and internal stress. Torque between adjacent links varies strongly with position.
explain.benefits: The only movable spatial four-bar with revolute joints, very few parts, and it can fold flat in some configurations for deployable structures.
explain.limits: Very sensitive to manufacturing errors and joint play, and its spatial motion is hard to use for ordinary machine tasks.

build.ground: link 1 (length a, twist alpha) holding hinge axes A and B
build.input: link 2 rotating about hinge axis B (angle th1)
build.output: link 4 rotating about hinge axis A (angle th2), and the folding shape of the loop

members.def: common normal a = 60 between axes A and B, twist alpha = 30°
common normal b = 100 between axes B and C, twist beta = 56.44°
a = 60, twist alpha = 30°, between C and D
b = 100, twist beta = 56.44°, between D and A

params.note: twist of links 2 and 4, from a/sin(alpha) = b/sin(beta)

Joint angles: th3 = -th1 (opposite joints equal and opposite), and tan(th1/2) tan(th2/2) = sin((beta + alpha)/2) / sin((beta - alpha)/2). The four axes lie on one hyperboloid of one sheet.

name: Swash plate
summary: A tilted disc on a shaft pushes a ring of pistons parallel to the shaft in and out once per turn, as in axial piston pumps.

ratio.typical: stroke = 2 R tan(gamma), 21.4 mm for R = 40, gamma = 15°

topology.notes: ground (cylinder block), shaft with swash plate, 5 pistons; each piston shoe slides on the plate face (higher pair)

explain.motion: A disc set at an angle gamma to the shaft rotates with it. Pistons arranged in a circle parallel to the shaft press against the disc face through slippers, so each piston moves in and out once per turn with simple harmonic motion, the pistons phased evenly round the circle. Changing gamma changes the stroke, and at zero angle the pistons stop.
explain.forces: Piston pressure force acts normal to the plate face, splitting into an axial thrust on the shaft bearing and a tangential part that makes the driving or driven torque. Shoe friction and the side load on pistons grow with the swash angle, which is why angles are kept below about 18°.
explain.benefits: Very compact, many pistons share one shaft for smooth flow, and the angle can be varied for displacement control.
explain.limits: Slipper and piston side loads limit the swash angle, and high-pressure contact faces need hydrostatic lubrication and clean fluid.

build.input: shaft with swash plate, continuous rotation

name: Flexure hinge
summary: A thin, bendable section of one solid part acts as a pivot, giving smooth, friction-free rotation over a small angle.

ratio.typical: rotation stiffness K = 2 E b t^2.5 / (9 pi R^0.5), about 13 N·m/rad here

topology.notes: one compliant joint modelled as a revolute with a torsional spring (pseudo-rigid-body model); in reality a single monolithic part

explain.motion: A circular notch cut from both sides of a solid bar leaves a thin neck. Applying a moment bends the neck, so the part beyond it rotates almost about the neck centre, as if pinned. The rotation is limited to a few degrees in metal, or much more in a polypropylene living hinge.
explain.forces: The hinge behaves like a torsional spring of stiffness K, so the driver must supply both the load torque and K times the angle. Bending stress peaks at the thinnest section and limits the safe angle; the neck is weak against off-axis loads and buckling.
explain.benefits: No friction, no backlash and no wear, no lubrication, and precise repeatable motion that can be cut in one piece by wire EDM or moulding.
explain.limits: Small range of motion, fatigue at the neck if overstressed, and the centre of rotation shifts slightly with load and angle.

build.ground: fixed block on one side of the notch
build.input: lever arm, moment or force at its tip rocking it about the neck
build.output: lever arm angle and tip displacement

members.def: rigid block left of the notch
rigid arm right of the notch, 60 long from neck centre to tip
circular notch radius R = 5, minimum thickness t = 0.8, width b = 10

name: Bistable compliant mechanism
summary: Flexible inclined beams hold a shuttle in either of two stable positions and snap it through the middle when pushed.

ratio.typical: two stable positions at ±L0 sin(theta0) = ±6.9 mm; snap-through at the centre

topology.notes: pseudo-rigid-body model: ground, shuttle, and two beams each split into two telescoping parts with an axial spring; flex ends as pins; shuttle on a guide. Real part is one piece

explain.motion: Two flexible beams angled from fixed anchors meet at a central shuttle. Pushing the shuttle toward the centre line compresses the beams, which store energy until the shuttle passes the middle, after which the beams push it on into the mirror-image stable position. It stays there with no power until pushed back.
explain.forces: Force rises from zero at a stable position to a peak, falls through zero at the unstable centre and becomes negative, so the shuttle snaps. The beams carry mostly axial compression, and peak strain occurs near the anchors and shuttle.
explain.benefits: Holds two positions with zero power, one-piece construction with no wear, and gives a crisp tactile switching action.
explain.limits: The snap can be violent and the switching force depends strongly on material and tolerance; plastic beams creep, lowering force over time.

build.ground: two anchors at x = ±39.4 mm, y = 0
build.output: shuttle position y, and its stable state

members.def: fixed ends of the beams at (±c, 0), c = L0 cos(theta0) = 39.4
left beam, free length L0 = 40, at theta0 = 10° in the as-made state
right beam, mirror of left
central block guided along y, joined to both beam ends

build.defining_relations: Beam length at shuttle height y: L(y) = sqrt(c^2 + y^2) with c = L0 cos(theta0). Force on shuttle F(y) = 2 ka (L0 - L(y)) y / L(y). Stable at y = ±h = ±L0 sin(theta0), unstable at y = 0. Stored energy U(y) = ka (L(y) - L0)^2.

build.notes: Animate as a quasi-static push then snap: when the input passes the force peak (at about y = ±4 mm here), jump the shuttle quickly to the far side. Bend the beams visually rather than telescoping them.

examples.detail: Light switches and power buttons with two positions and no separate spring.
Microscale bistable beams hold an optical or electrical switch state without power.

name: Centrifugal governor
summary: Spinning weights swing out as speed rises and lift a sleeve that can close a throttle, holding an engine near a set speed.

ratio.typical: ball height below pivot h = g / omega^2 (Watt type)

topology.notes: frame, spindle, 2 ball arms, 2 links, sleeve; sleeve slides on the spindle; dof 2 = spindle speed plus ball height, the height settled by dynamics

explain.motion: Two balls on arms hinged at the top of a vertical spindle are swung round by the engine. As speed rises they fly outward and upward like a conical pendulum, and links from the arms pull a sleeve up the spindle. The sleeve moves a lever that closes the steam valve or opens it again when speed falls.
explain.forces: Centrifugal force on each ball, m omega^2 times its radius, balances gravity and the sleeve load through the arm angle. The sleeve can supply only a small force, and friction in the sleeve and valve linkage makes the governor insensitive to small speed changes.
explain.benefits: Automatic feedback speed control with no external power, simple and robust, and a classic visual of control engineering.
explain.limits: The plain Watt governor has small sleeve force and changes speed setting with load (proportional droop), and can hunt or oscillate. Not usable at high speeds without springs or dead weights (Porter, Hartnell types).

build.input: spindle, driven at engine speed omega about the vertical axis
build.output: sleeve height on the spindle (and arm angle phi)

examples.detail: Watt's engines from the 1780s used a flyball governor to throttle steam to hold speed.

name: Ball-and-disc integrator
summary: A ball set at an adjustable radius on a turning disc drives an output roller, so the output angle is the integral of the radius.

ratio.typical: omega_out = omega_disc x x / r_c, reversing through zero at the disc centre

topology.notes: ground, disc, carriage, ball, output cylinder; ball rolls on disc and cylinder and is held in the carriage cage

explain.motion: A flat disc turns with the input variable, say time. A ball pressed onto its face is held by a carriage at distance x from the disc centre, and the ball also touches a cylinder whose axis is parallel to the carriage travel. The ball turns at a speed proportional to x, so the cylinder angle accumulates the integral of x over the disc angle, and moving the ball past the centre reverses it.
explain.forces: Only a small torque can be passed by rolling friction, so the output must be very lightly loaded or followed by a torque amplifier. Sliding across the contact when the carriage moves causes slight error and wear.
explain.benefits: Solves integration continuously and exactly in principle with simple parts, and allows smooth reversal through zero.
explain.limits: Very low output torque, slip errors under load, and accuracy depends on flat, clean, hard surfaces.

name: Friction wheel drive
summary: A rubber-rimmed wheel pressed on the face of a spinning disc turns faster the farther out it sits, giving a stepless, reversible ratio.

ratio.typical: omega_w / omega_d = R / r_w, 0.5 to 3.0 here; through zero to reverse

topology.notes: ground, disc, wheel on a splined shaft; the wheel's position along its shaft is a ratio setting (extra slide not counted)

explain.motion: The engine turns a flat disc. A wheel with a rubber or fibre rim presses on the disc face and can slide along its own shaft, which runs across the disc. Near the centre the wheel turns slowly, far out it turns fast, and moving it past the centre reverses it.
explain.forces: Torque transmitted is limited to mu x normal force x contact radius on the disc side. A spring or lever keeps the wheel pressed on; the high normal force loads both bearings. Different parts of the contact patch move at different speeds, causing scrubbing, heat and rim wear.
explain.benefits: Stepless, reversible ratio with very few parts, and it slips safely on overload.
explain.limits: Low power capacity, rim wear and glazing, slip in wet or oily conditions, and efficiency drops at small radii.

build.ground: frame with disc bearing and wheel shaft bearings
build.output: friction wheel rotation; its contact radius R is the ratio setting

members.def: flat disc radius 100
rubber-rimmed wheel radius r_w = 30, slides on a splined shaft along a disc radius
bearings, wheel shaft axis lies parallel to the disc face 30 above it and crosses the disc axis

build.defining_relations: omega_w = omega_d R / r_w (sign follows R). Max torque on wheel T = mu N r_w. Power limit P = mu N omega_d R.
build.range: disc continuous; R from 15 to 90 gives 0.5 to 3.0 x disc speed; R negative reverses
build.plot: wheel speed vs contact radius setting
build.notes: Animate the shift as a slider moving the wheel along its shaft. Show the speed mismatch across the wheel width as small arrows to explain scrubbing.

name: Belt CVT (variable pulley)
summary: Two V-pulleys with movable cone halves change their working diameters together, so a belt gives a stepless ratio.

ratio.typical: about 0.4:1 to 2.5:1 here (spread about 6.2); car CVTs typically spread 5 to 7

topology.notes: ground, input shaft with fixed sheave, input movable sheave, output shaft with fixed sheave, output movable sheave, belt; movable sheaves slide on splines; ratio setting is a second, controlled freedom

explain.motion: Each pulley is a pair of cones; one cone can slide along the shaft. Squeezing the input cones together pushes the belt outward to a larger radius, while the output cones spread so the belt sinks inward, which raises the output speed. Because the belt length is fixed, the two radii change together and the ratio moves smoothly between the limits.
explain.forces: Torque is carried by friction between the belt flanks and the sheave cones, so large clamping forces, from springs, flyweights or hydraulics, are needed. A steel push belt transmits by compression between its elements; rubber belts by tension.
explain.benefits: Keeps the engine at its best speed with no shift steps, simple to automate, and smooth.
explain.limits: Torque is limited by clamping force and belt strength, efficiency is a few percent below gears, and belts wear or slip if overloaded.
